_note: PROVISIONAL. These groups are a conservative inference from 'pulmonary condition', NOT her doctor's instructions. Replace message_en and add groups from her actual medical advice before relying on this (plan Task 12 step 3). Wording is deliberately 'is named on this packaging' and never 'contains' — a Korean box names other drugs in its contraindication paragraph, so a match does not prove containment.

rules.message_en: An NSAID — or a product known to include one — is named on this packaging. NSAIDs can trigger breathing problems in some people with asthma and related conditions. Show this box to the pharmacist and ask whether acetaminophen (아세트아미노펜) is suitable for you. This includes patches and gels, not only tablets.
rules.source: GINA 2025 report, NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease; Korean OTC analgesic product inserts

rules.message_en: An opioid cough suppressant is named on this packaging. Opioids can slow breathing, which matters more with a lung condition. Do not take this before asking your doctor or pharmacist about your condition.
rules.source: Dihydrocodeine appears in widely sold Korean OTC cough and cold products; standard opioid respiratory-depression caution in chronic respiratory disease

rules.message_en: A non-selective beta-blocker is named on this packaging. These can narrow the airways, and that applies to eye drops as well as tablets. Do not start this without asking your doctor or pharmacist about your lung condition.
rules.source: Standard contraindication guidance for non-selective beta-blockers in obstructive airway disease, including ophthalmic timolol, carteolol and levobunolol

rules.message_en: A pyrazolone painkiller — or a Korean brand known to include one — is named on this packaging. These are associated with analgesic-induced asthma. Ask the pharmacist for an alternative and mention your lung condition.
rules.source: Isopropylantipyrine is an ingredient of the Korean OTC analgesics 게보린 and 사리돈; analgesic-induced asthma literature

rules.message_en: A decongestant — oral or nasal — is named on this packaging. Decongestants can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and nasal sprays rebound if used for more than a few days. Tell the pharmacist about your lung condition and any other medicines you take before using this.
rules.source: Korean product inserts for OTC cold remedies and nasal sprays; standard sympathomimetic decongestant cautions

rules.message_en: A sulfite preservative is named on this packaging. Sulfites are a recognised asthma trigger for some people, and they appear in food and drink as well as medicines. If you have reacted to dried fruit or wine before, ask your doctor whether to avoid this.
rules.source: Sulfite-sensitive asthma is well documented; Korean food labelling lists 아황산염 among allergens

rules.message_en: A sedating antihistamine is named on this packaging. These cause drowsiness and can thicken airway secretions. Ask the pharmacist whether a non-drowsy alternative would suit you better.
rules.source: Korean OTC antihistamine product inserts; standard first-generation antihistamine cautions
